objectives: Given two or three business ideas, score each idea on your skills, time, start-up cost and local demand, and choose one, using the same scores for every idea and writing why the winner fits

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing a business that fits your life
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Score two or three business ideas and choose the one that fits you best.
This lesson builds toward: Given two or three business ideas, you will score each idea on your skills, time, start-up cost and local demand, and choose one, using the same scores for every idea and writing why the winner fits.
The best business for you is one that people nearby want, that uses skills you have, and that fits the time and money you really have. A business that needs you at the market from 5 am may not fit if you take children to school.
Write two or three ideas. Score each from 1 (poor) to 3 (good) on four things: your skills, the time it needs compared with the time you have, the start-up cost compared with the money you have, and local demand (do people buy this nearby, and is there room for one more seller?). Add the scores.
Example: Halima in Kaduna scores three ideas. Selling kunu drinks near a school: skills 3, time 2, cost 3, demand 3 = 11. Tailoring: skills 2, time 2, cost 1, demand 2 = 7. Selling phone credit: skills 2, time 3, cost 2, demand 1 = 8 (many sellers already). She chooses the drinks. Aïcha in Dakar might score a thiakry dessert stall, hair braiding and a small boutique the same way.
Scores help you think; they do not decide for you. Also ask: would I enjoy this, and can I grow it later?
Step by step:
- Write two or three ideas.
- Score each 1 to 3 on skills, time, start-up cost and local demand.
- Add the scores.
- Choose one and write why it fits your life.
Words to know:
- Start-up cost: the money you need to begin: tools, first stock, a stall or a licence.
- Demand: how many people want to buy something, and how much.
Try it now: Write two or three business ideas. Score each 1 to 3 on skills, time, start-up cost and local demand, add the scores, and write one sentence on why your top idea fits your life.
You can now compare business ideas with simple scores and choose one that fits your life.

check.q: Which four things do you score each idea on?
options: Skills, time, start-up cost and local demand
What friends like, weather, music, fashion
Only how much money it might make
check.why: Skills, time, cost and demand show whether an idea fits you and your market.

check.q: An idea scores high on skills but there are already ten sellers on your street. Which score is low?
check.why: Many sellers nearby means less room for one more, so demand is low.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Testing your idea with real customers
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Test an idea with a small batch and at least ten real customers before spending big.
This lesson builds toward: Before spending most of your money on a new idea, you will test the idea with a small batch and at least ten real customers, writing down how many bought, the price they paid and one change to make.
Many businesses fail because the owner spends all her savings before knowing if people will buy. Test small first: make or buy a small batch, offer it to real customers, and watch what happens.
Make a small batch, for example 20 cups of zobo, 5 dresses or 10 hair appointments. Offer it to at least ten people who are not close family. Write down: how many bought, the price they paid, what they liked, and what they asked for. People's actions matter more than polite words: "I will buy next week" is not a sale.
Example: Esther in Kisumu tests liquid soap. She makes 15 bottles, sells 12 at KES 150 (an example price), and three customers ask for a bigger bottle. Her change: add a bigger size. A woman in Alexandria testing home-made pickles could do the same with neighbours and a small shop.
After the test, decide: go ahead, change something, or try your next idea. A test that fails costs little and saves you a lot.
Step by step:
- Make or buy a small batch.
- Offer it to at least ten people who are not close family.
- Write how many bought, the price, what they liked and what they asked for.
- Decide: go ahead, change one thing, or try the next idea.
Words to know:
- Small batch: a small amount made or bought to test before making more.
- Test: trying an idea on a small scale to learn before spending a lot.
Try it now: Plan a test for your chosen idea: what small batch you will make, the price you will try, and ten people you will offer it to this week. After the test, write how many bought and one change to make.
You can now test a business idea cheaply with real customers and decide what to do next.

check.q: What is the best proof that customers want your product?
options: Your mother says it is nice
Friends say they will buy next month
People who are not family pay for it
check.why: Real sales to real customers show true demand.

check.q: Your test sells 3 of 20 items. What is a good next step?
options: Ask buyers what to change, change one thing, and test again
Spend all your savings on more stock
check.why: A weak test is a cheap lesson: learn, change one thing and try again.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Pricing for profit and paying yourself
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate the cost per item, set a price with profit, and set an amount to pay yourself.
This lesson builds toward: Given the costs of one product or service, you will calculate the cost per item, set a price with a profit, and set an amount to pay yourself, with every cost included and the arithmetic correct.
Many women underprice, especially when selling to neighbours, and work hard for no real profit. Count every cost: ingredients or materials, packaging, transport, charcoal or gas, phone data, a stall fee, and your own time.
Cost per item = total cost of a batch divided by the number of items. Then add a profit. Example from Kumasi: Abena makes 40 meat pies. Flour, meat, oil and gas cost GHS 160, bags GHS 10 and transport GHS 10: GHS 180 in total, so GHS 4.50 per pie. She sells at GHS 7 (example figures), so each pie earns GHS 2.50 profit. Check that customers will pay your price by looking at similar sellers.
Pay yourself. Decide a set amount you take from the business each week, and leave the rest in the business for stock and growth. If you take everything, the business cannot grow; if you take nothing, you are working for free. Write what you take in your records.
If your price does not cover your costs, change something: a smaller size, a better supplier, buying in bulk with others, or a higher price for better quality.
Step by step:
- List every cost of one batch, including transport, fuel, data and fees.
- Divide the total by the number of items to get the cost per item.
- Add a profit to set the price; compare with similar sellers.
- Decide a set weekly amount to pay yourself; leave the rest in the business.
Words to know:
- Cost per item: the total cost of a batch divided by the number of items made.
- Profit: the money left after all costs are paid.
- Paying yourself: a set amount the owner takes from the business, so the rest stays for stock and growth.
Try it now: Pick one product. List every cost of one batch, work out the cost per item, set a price with a profit, and decide how much you will pay yourself each week.
You can now price a product so it makes a profit and pay yourself a set amount.

check.q: A batch of 20 bags costs 10,000 NGN in total. What is the cost per bag?
check.why: 10,000 divided by 20 is 500 NGN per bag.

check.q: Why pay yourself a set amount instead of taking all the money?
options: So money stays in the business for stock and growth
It is required by every bank
check.why: A set amount pays you and leaves money to keep the business going and growing.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Making time: family, care and support
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Draw up a weekly time plan with business hours, care duties and who helps.
This lesson builds toward: Given your work and home duties for one week, you will draw up a weekly time plan that shows business hours, care duties and who will help, agreed with at least one family member or helper.
Women in many places do most of the unpaid care work at home: cooking, cleaning, fetching water, and caring for children, the sick and elders. UN Women notes this leaves women less time for paid work. A business needs time too, so plan it.
Draw a week: seven days and morning, afternoon and evening. Mark care duties, then your business hours: buying stock, making, selling, answering messages and records. Look for clashes and gaps.
Then ask for help. Talk with your husband or partner, older children, a sister or a neighbour about sharing tasks such as fetching water, school runs or cooking on busy market days. Some women swap childcare with other mothers, or work near home on some days. Example: Mariam in Yaoundé sells at the market Tuesday, Friday and Saturday; her sister takes the children on those mornings and Mariam does her sister's hair in return.
Show the plan to your family and agree on it. Look after yourself too: rest and health keep the business going.
Step by step:
- Draw seven days with morning, afternoon and evening.
- Mark care and household duties.
- Mark business hours: buying, making, selling, messages, records.
- Find clashes and ask a family member or helper to share tasks.
- Agree the plan together and include rest.
Words to know:
- Unpaid care work: work at home that is not paid, such as cooking, cleaning and caring for children, the sick and elders.
- Childcare swap: mothers taking turns to look after each other's children.
Official sources:
- UN Women: economic empowerment (unpaid care work, access to assets and finance)
Try it now: Draw your weekly time plan with care duties and business hours. Mark one clash, write who could help with it, and talk with that person this week.
You can now plan your week so your business and your care duties fit, with the support you need.

check.q: Your market day clashes with the school run. What is a good step?
options: Ask a family member or another mother to share the school run
check.why: Sharing tasks frees time for the business without harming the family.

check.q: Why show your time plan to your family?
options: So they can agree and help
So they can take your money
check.why: When the family agrees the plan, they are more likely to help.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Finding money and support safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check that a loan, grant or programme is real and keep control of your money.
This lesson builds toward: When you look for a loan, grant or support programme, you will check that the offer is real on the official site and keep control of your own money and PIN, paying no "processing fee" to strangers and sharing your PIN with no one.
There are programmes for women and small businesses. Examples: Kenya's Women Enterprise Fund, a government fund for women's enterprises; Nigeria's SMEDAN, whose free registration opens programmes such as the Women In Self-employment Programme; Senegal's DER/FJ, which offers training, formalisation and financing for women and young people; the Ghana Enterprises Agency; and the African Development Bank's AFAWA initiative, which works with banks and lenders to help them lend to women. Savings groups and microfinance are covered in their own course.
Names, rules and open dates change, so always check on the programme's official website or office. Scammers pretend to offer women's grants and loans and ask for a "processing" or "registration" fee first. A real programme tells you its fees on its official site; never pay a stranger to get a grant.
Keep control of your money. Have your own mobile money line or account in your name, and keep your PIN secret from everyone, including family. A real provider never asks for your PIN. If someone takes your earnings by force or threats, that is abuse; talk to a person you trust, a women's group or a local support service.
Before you borrow, know the total you must repay, when, and what happens if you are late. Borrow for something that will earn money, not to cover daily household costs.
Step by step:
- Find the programme's official website or office.
- Check what it offers, who can apply, and its open dates and fees.
- Refuse anyone who asks for a fee to stranger accounts.
- Keep a mobile money line or account in your own name and a secret PIN.
- Before borrowing, write the total to repay, when, and the late rules.
Words to know:
- Grant: money given for a purpose that does not have to be paid back.
- Loan: money borrowed that must be paid back, usually with extra cost (interest).
- Advance-fee scam: a trick where someone promises money but asks you to pay a fee first.
Official sources:
- Women Enterprise Fund, Kenya (government fund for women's enterprises)
- SMEDAN, Nigeria: free registration, SME Digital Academy and programmes including the Women In Self-employment Programme
- DER/FJ, Senegal: Délégation générale à l'Entreprenariat Rapide des Femmes et des Jeunes (formalisation, training, financing)
- Ghana Enterprises Agency: support for micro and small enterprises
- African Development Bank: AFAWA, Affirmative Finance Action for Women in Africa
Try it now: Pick one programme from this lesson or one you know. Find its official website or office, and write what it offers, who can apply, whether it is open now, and the date you checked.
You can now find support for your business, check that it is real, and keep control of your own money.

check.q: A message says you won a women's business grant; pay 5,000 KES "processing fee" first. What is this?
options: A scam; check the official site and pay no stranger
check.why: Asking for a fee before giving a grant is a classic advance-fee scam.

check.q: Who should know your mobile money PIN?
check.why: Your PIN protects your money; a real provider never asks for it.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Networks, mentors and a six-month growth plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write three measurable goals for six months and name one mentor or group to contact.
This lesson builds toward: For the next six months, you will write three measurable business goals and name one mentor, group or association to contact, each goal with a number and a date.
Many women grow faster with others: a mentor who has done it, a women's business association, a market or trade association, a cooperative, a chamber of commerce or a business support centre. They share buyers, suppliers, advice and courage.
A mentor is someone more experienced who gives you advice. Ask a woman you admire for 20 minutes of advice, with two clear questions. Join one group where your customers or suppliers meet. Attend a trade fair or market day in a bigger town when you can.
Then write three goals for the next six months. Make each one measurable, with a number and a date: "Sell 60 bottles of soap a week by the end of March", "Save GHS 500 for a second sewing machine by June" (an example figure), "Get five new shop customers by May". Check your goals once a month and write what you did.
Example: Ngozi in Enugu, who sells Ankara bags, joins a women's traders association, finds a mentor who exports bags, and sets goals for sales, savings and her first stall at a trade fair.
Step by step:
- List people and groups who could help: mentors, associations, cooperatives, support centres.
- Choose one to contact this month, with two clear questions.
- Write three goals, each with a number and a date.
- Check your goals once a month and write what you did.
Words to know:
- Mentor: an experienced person who gives you advice and support.
- Measurable goal: a goal with a number and a date, so you can see if you reached it.
- Association: a group of people in the same trade or situation who support each other.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page business plan with your scored idea, test results, price and profit, what you pay yourself, your weekly time plan, one checked support option, three six-month goals and one mentor or group to contact.
You can now build a network and write a six-month growth plan with measurable goals.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Idea chosen One idea with no scores, or scores without reasons. Two or three ideas scored on skills, time, cost and demand, with a reason the winner fits. Also notes how the idea could grow later. Idea tested No test, or only family asked. A small batch offered to at least ten real customers, with sales, price and one change written down. The change was made and tested a second time. Price, profit and pay Costs missing, wrong arithmetic, or no amount to pay yourself. Every cost listed, correct cost per item, a price with profit, and a set weekly amount to pay yourself. Price compared with similar sellers, with a plan if costs rise. Time plan and support No time plan, or no help named. A weekly plan with business hours, care duties and who helps, agreed with at least one person. Includes rest and a backup helper. Finance and support checked safely An option from a forwarded message or a stranger, or a PIN shared. One option checked on its official site, with who can apply and the date checked; money kept in your own name. Also writes the total to repay, when, and late rules for any loan. Goals and network Vague goals, or no mentor or group named. Three goals with numbers and dates, and one mentor or group to contact. The contact was made and the first monthly check is planned. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: "Sell 40 dresses a month by the end of June"
check.why: It has a number and a date, so you can check if you reached it.

check.q: How do you ask a possible mentor for help?
options: Ask for 20 minutes with two clear questions
Ask her to give you money
Ask her to run your business
check.why: A short, clear request respects her time and gets useful advice.
